rows.title: PHYSICAL ANTHROPOLOGY
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
objectives: Objective Describe the scientific process as a methodology for understanding the natural world, including the steps in the scientific process and the meaning of theory in science.

Objective Define the scope of anthropology and distinguish cultural, archaeology, linguistic and physical anthropology (including dental anthropology, primatology, paleoanthropology, paleopathology, and forensic anthropology).
Objective Identify key historical figures whose concepts provide a foundation for evolutionary theory.
Objective Explain the basic principles of cell structure, DNA, and cell division.
Objective Explain the basic principles of Mendelian and polygenic traits.

Objective Explain the basic principles of modern evolutionary theory (gene flow, mutation, genetic drift and recombination) which produce and distribute genetic variation and the role of natural selection.
Objective Demonstrate an understanding of the classification of living primates: A. Mammalian traits B. Primate physical traits C. Habitats D.Dentition and diet E. Locomotion
Objective Demonstrate an understanding of primate taxonomy: A. Prosimians (lemurs, lorises) B. Tarsiers C. Anthropoids (monkeys, apes and humans) D. Hominoids (apes and humans) E. Hominins

Objective Demonstrate an understanding of nonhuman primate behavior: A. Captive and wild studies B. Dominance hierarchies C. Communication D. Affiliative behavior E. Aggression F. Reproduction G. Mothers and infants H. Cultural behavior I. Human threats J. Primate continuum
Objective Summarize methods used in interpreting the fossil record: A. Processes of fossilization B. Taphonomy C. Relative and chronometric dating techniques

Objective Recognize major groups in nonhuman primate evolutionary history and provide alternate phylogenies: A. Principles of classification B. Vertebrate evolutionary history C. Mammalian evolution D. Miocene fossil hominoids E. Modes of evolutionary change

Objective Recognize major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution: A. Definition of hominid B. Bipedal adaptations C. Biocultural evolution D. Paleoanthropology a multidisciplinary approach E. Pre-Australopithecines F. South and East African Australopithecus G. South and East African Paranthropus H. Early Homo I. Taxonomic challenges

Objective Recognize major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution (Homo ergaster/erectus and contemporaries): A. Homo ergaster morphology, diet and tool use. B. Homo erectus morphology, diet and tool use. C. Homo georgicus morphology, diet and tool use

Objective Recognize major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution (Neandertals and Archaic Homo sapiens): A. Homo heidelbergensis morphology, diet, tool use, and taxonomy B. Neandertal morphology, sites, tool technology, culture, symbolic behavior, diet, burials, genetic evidence

Objective Recognize major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution (Homo sapiens): A. Origin and dispersal of anatomically modern humans B. Site locations and estimated ages C. Technology and symbolic expression in Upper Paleolithic

Objective Identify biological and cultural factors responsible for modern human variation and adaptation: A. Concepts of “race” B. Human biocultural evolution C. Population genetics D. Contemporary interpretations of human variation and its adaptive significance E. Impact of infectious disease F. Growth and development (genetics, hormones, environmental factors, cultural factors)
Objective Identify the issues facing humanity: A. Loss of biodiversity B. Overpopulation C. Famine D. Environmental changes

rows.title: ASTRONOMY
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
objectives: Objective Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to: 1. Explain and coordinate systems used in astronomy and how/why each is used: a. longitude and latitude b. altitude and azimuth c. right ascension and declination 2. Describe the motions of the sun and moon as seen from the earth and as seen from outside the earth. 3. Explain the causes of the seasons, the phases of the moon, and the motions of the stars and planets. 4. Use a star chart to recognize astronomical objects and describe the motions of the sun and moon. 5. Explain the difference between and usefulness of sidereal and solar time. 6. Describe the Ptolemaic System. 7. Describe the Copernican System. 8. Explain contributions of certain astronomers. 9. Describe the laws of force, motion and gravitation. 10. Explain the difference between speculation, hypothesis, theories, and observations. 11. Explain the difference between belief in an idea and scientific proof. 12. Describe characteristics of each of the planets and their satellite systems. 13. Describe how to calculate the size of a planet given the distance to the planet and its subtended angle. 14. Calculate various properties of the ellipse. 15. Explain how information is gleaned from the light of distant objects. 16. Explain why stars have different brightnesses. 17. Describe the physical processes occurring inside stars. 18. Explain how we know the distances to some stars. 19. Explain why stars evolve and what they evolve into. 20. Calculate the distances to stars, knowing their apparent and absolute magnitudes. 21. Describe the contents of our Milky Way galaxy and explain how they are related to the galaxy's evolution. 22. Recognize other galaxies and describe their basic properties. 23. Explain the evidence for an expanding universe. 24. Explain the possible origins and fate of the universe.
Astronomical reference systems of the sky.
Motions in the sky of the sun, moon, planets, and stars.
Early theories of the solar system. (Ptolemy, Copernicus)
Laws of planetary motion and gravity. (Kepler, Galileo, Newton)

Physical processes in other normal and peculiar galaxies.
